title: SYSK Selects: How Patents Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun (originally November 2014) explaining how patents work. The hosts cover the constitutional basis for patents, the history of early English and US patents (including King Henry VI's 1449 patent, Samuel Hopkins as first US patent holder, and Lincoln's only patent), and how patents differ from copyright, trademarks, trade secrets and service marks. They explain the novelty, non-obviousness and usefulness requirements, utility, design and plant patent types and their terms, and the application process (search, patent attorney or agent, application, claims, rejection and refiling, first-to-file rule). They also discuss criticisms: patent trolls, submarine patents (Jerome Lemelson), backlog at the Patent and Trade Office, unused patents, employee invention ownership, and drug patent blocking. The episode closes with a listener mail about panic attacks and college mental health services.

entities.name: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.title: Rerun intro
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects episode on how patents work, noting it is from November 2014, and the hosts begin with banter about the new year and whether either has patents.

segments.title: Constitutional basis and early patent history
segments.summary: The hosts cite the Intellectual Property Clause in Article One, Section Eight of the Constitution. They trace early English patents to King Henry VI's 1449 grant to John of Utynam for stained glass, and the abuses that led to the 1624 statute. They then cover the first US patent to Samuel Hopkins for potash, Jefferson's role reviewing patents, and the creation of the US patent office in 1802.

segments.title: Famous patent holders
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Abraham Lincoln as the only president to hold a patent, for a device to lift boats off sandbars, and Mark Twain's patents, including an adjustable brass strap for garments, a history memory game, and a self-pasting scrapbook.

segments.title: Patents vs. copyright, trademark, trade secret and service mark
segments.summary: The hosts explain that copyright is automatic and lasts for the author's life plus seventy years, trademarks protect brand names and designs, and trade secrets such as the Coke formula can be kept indefinitely. A service mark covers services rather than products. A patent protects an actual invention and its design, and the patent is published, so it expires after twenty years.

segments.title: Requirements for patentability
segments.summary: The hosts explain that an invention must be novel, non-obvious and useful. Examples include the cam-corder patented by Jerome Lemelson in 1977, a toaster with extra slots as obvious, and a random gear arrangement as not useful. Inventions that serve only immoral purposes may also be refused, and natural discoveries like Einstein's relativity cannot be patented.

segments.title: Patent types and terms
segments.summary: The hosts describe utility patents, which cover processes, machines, manufactures, compositions of matter and improvements, and last twenty years. Design patents, such as for a chair or shoe design, last fourteen years. Plant patents cover asexually reproducible plants and last twenty years. The 2014 Supreme Court ruling on human genes and Australia's contrasting approach are also covered.

segments.title: Edison, Lemelson and submarine patents
segments.summary: Edison held 1,093 US patents and ran a Menlo Park research factory. Lemelson held 557 and is accused of submarine patent litigation through his foundation, which collected about a billion dollars before a judge applied a reasonable statute of limitations to barcode cases. The hosts mention TRIPS and TiVo as related points.

segments.title: Patent trolls, reform and the broken system
segments.summary: The hosts describe how courts have swung toward patent holders, creating patent trolls who buy vague patents, especially software ones, and sue for settlements. They discuss the Innovation Act, which passed the House and stalled in the Senate, the tech industry versus pharmaceutical industry debate, and accidental versus willful infringement. They also cite research on unused patents and the Patent Office backlog.

segments.title: How to file a patent
segments.summary: The hosts outline the steps: searching existing patents, hiring a patent attorney or agent, filing an application that includes prior art, a summary, a preferred embodiment and claims, and paying fees. The patent term begins at filing. They mention the cost estimates, the sliding fee schedule, and Invent Help and the Lemelson Foundation as resources.

segments.title: Rejections, employee inventions and drug patents
segments.summary: The hosts explain that applications are often rejected on the first pass and can be revised and refiled. They discuss employees whose inventions belong to their companies, the Superman creators, and the Rudolph copyright story. They also cover drug companies that sit on patents, such as the Amgen case, and the interference process and first-to-file rule that replaced the older system in 2013.

segments.title: Poor man's copyright myth
segments.summary: The hosts say the poor man's copyright, mailing an invention to yourself, is an old wives' tale that would not hold up in court, and that patenting quickly is the best defense.

segments.title: Listener mail: panic attacks and college therapy
segments.summary: A listener writes about college panic attacks, therapy and medication through their university's health services, and urges students to use campus mental health services. Josh and Chuck thank the listener and close with contact information.
